rules.title: One primary action per surface
rules.statement: Give each section, card or dialog at most one primary-styled action.
rules.why: When two actions share the strongest style, people stop to compare them and neither reads as the next step. One primary action makes the intended path obvious; everything else becomes secondary or a link.
rules.check: Count primary-styled actions per section and dialog at 1440 and 390: one at most.
rules.anti_pattern: A hero with two equally filled buttons ("Get started" and "Book a demo"), or the same filled button repeated on every card in a grid.
sources: design.md §3 (principle 4: one primary action per surface)

items.title: Pricing tiers compared on the limits that matter

rules.title: Headings follow the outline
rules.statement: One h1 per page; nest h2–h4 in order. Level follows structure, size follows style.
rules.why: Screen-reader users move through a page by its headings, so the outline is its table of contents. Choosing a level for its default size breaks that outline and makes a component wrong as soon as it is reused elsewhere.
rules.check: Run axe heading-order or list the outline: one h1, no skipped levels.
rules.anti_pattern: Every section title an h2 regardless of nesting, card titles that jump from h2 to h5 to get a smaller font, or styled divs standing in for headings.
sources: docs/quality-gates.md (Accessibility: semantic landmarks and heading order)

items.title: Empty state that says why and what next
FAQ that answers real objections

rules.title: One eyebrow at most
rules.statement: Use at most one uppercase eyebrow per page, and only if it adds information.
rules.why: A tracked-out label over every heading adds a layer of hierarchy that carries no information, and it is one of the most recognisable marks of generated UI. A heading that makes its point needs no label.
rules.check: Count uppercase, letter-spaced labels over headings: one per page at most.
rules.anti_pattern: A small accent-coloured "FEATURES", "PRICING" or "FAQ" label above every section heading.
sources: docs/v1.2/plan.md §4 (tells: one eyebrow, in the hero only)

rules.title: Numbers only for sequences
rules.statement: Use numbered markers (01, 02, Step 1) only for steps people follow in order.
rules.why: Numbers promise an order. On things that can be read in any order they add noise and send readers looking for a progression that isn't there.
rules.check: For each numbered marker: does order matter to the user? If not, drop the numbers.
rules.anti_pattern: Three feature cards labelled 01, 02 and 03 that could be read in any order.
sources: docs/v1.2/plan.md §4 (tells: numbered markers only for real sequences)

rules.title: Readable line length
rules.statement: Cap running text at a readable measure (about 65ch), never the full container width.
rules.why: Long lines make the eye lose its place on the return sweep; very short ones break phrases apart. A fixed measure keeps text readable however wide the screen is.
rules.check: At 1440, every body paragraph has a max-width of 80ch or less.
rules.anti_pattern: A paragraph stretched across a 1280px container, or a hero description inheriting the full page width.
sources: WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.8 Visual Presentation (AAA: no more than 80 characters)

rules.title: Few sizes, from one scale
rules.statement: Take font sizes from the type scale; use at most four sizes in one section.
rules.why: Hierarchy reads clearly when each size step means something. One-off sizes blur the steps and drift apart between components.
rules.check: List computed font sizes per section at 1440 and 390: all on the scale, four at most.
rules.anti_pattern: Arbitrary values such as text-[15px] and text-[13.5px] chosen per component, with five or six sizes competing in one card.

rules.title: Tabular figures for compared numbers
rules.statement: Set prices, counts and numeric columns in tabular figures.
rules.why: Proportional digits have different widths, so columns of numbers don't line up and values jitter when they update. Tabular figures keep every digit the same width.
rules.check: Inspect prices, counts and numeric columns: font-variant-numeric is tabular-nums.
rules.anti_pattern: Prices and table totals in proportional figures, so columns zig-zag and a live counter shifts as it changes.
sources: docs/quality-gates.md (Visual and type: tabular numbers for counts)

items.title: Pricing tiers compared on the limits that matter

rules.title: Group by proximity
rules.statement: Keep space inside a group smaller than space between groups, at every width.
rules.why: Space is how people see what belongs together. When a heading sits as far from its paragraph as from the previous section, the structure has to be read instead of seen.
rules.check: Measure gaps at 1440 and 390: label to content < item to item < section to section.
rules.anti_pattern: One uniform gap applied to everything, so headings float between sections instead of attaching to their content.

rules.title: One shared edge
rules.statement: Align a section's heading, text and actions on one left edge; centre only short blocks.
rules.why: A shared edge gives the eye one line to scan down. Centring everything starts every line at a different place, which slows reading and leaves long text and lists ragged on both sides.
rules.check: At 1440, heading, text and actions share a left edge; centred text runs 3 lines at most.
rules.anti_pattern: Every section centred: centred heading, centred paragraph, centred cards and centred buttons, whatever their length.

items.title: Empty state that says why and what next
FAQ that answers real objections

rules.title: Density fits the task
rules.statement: Make data surfaces compact and reading surfaces roomy; don't use one density everywhere.
rules.why: Data is scanned and compared, so every extra pixel of padding hides a row. Marketing and reading surfaces are read once and need air. One density everywhere fails one of the two.
rules.check: At 1440×900, data rows are 48px tall or less; reading text has line-height 1.5 or more.
rules.anti_pattern: Data tables with card-sized rows and generous padding, or landing sections packed edge to edge like a spreadsheet.
sources: AGENTS.md §13, v1.1 (tag v1.1-archive): research and database surfaces may be denser than marketing surfaces

rules.title: Semantic tokens only
rules.statement: Colour with semantic tokens (background, primary, muted, border…), never raw values.
rules.why: Raw colours lock a component to one palette and break dark mode and the installing project's theme. Semantic roles let the same structure work in any theme.
rules.check: No hex, rgb(), hsl() or palette classes in the component; it works in light and dark.
rules.anti_pattern: Hard-coded hex values, Tailwind palette classes such as text-gray-500 and white cards that ignore the project's theme and vanish in dark mode.

rules.title: Never colour alone
rules.statement: Pair every colour-coded meaning (error, selected, status) with text or shape.
rules.why: Colour alone fails people with colour-vision deficiencies, monochrome screens and forced-colours mode. A text label also gives screen readers the meaning.
rules.check: View it in greyscale: every state is still identifiable from text or shape.
rules.anti_pattern: A red border as the only sign of an error, or a highlighted card as the only sign of the recommended plan.

items.title: Empty state that says why and what next
Pricing tiers compared on the limits that matter

rules.title: The accent is scarce
rules.statement: Spend the primary colour on the primary action and real status, not decoration.
rules.why: An accent works because it is rare. When icons, headings, borders and backgrounds all use it, nothing stands out and the primary action loses its pull.
rules.check: At 1440 and 390, every element in the primary colour is the primary action or a status.
rules.anti_pattern: Primary-coloured icons on every card, tinted section backgrounds, gradient headings and accent-coloured text everywhere.
sources: design.md §6 (usage rules: accent kept to a small share of the viewport)

rules.title: No effects as emphasis
rules.statement: Show importance with position, size, weight and borders, not gradients, glows or glass.
rules.why: Effects cost contrast, render differently across themes and date quickly. They are also the usual way generated UI fakes emphasis the structure doesn't have.
rules.check: Search the styles for gradients, blur and backdrop-filter: none carries meaning.
rules.anti_pattern: A gradient border and glow around the "Most popular" plan, glass cards over a blurred blob, gradient text in the hero.
sources: design.md §15 (AI gradients, glassmorphism, oversized blur glows)
AGENTS.md §13, v1.1 (tag v1.1-archive): no glassmorphism or glow gradients

items.title: Pricing tiers compared on the limits that matter

rules.title: Native elements first
rules.statement: Use the native element (button, a, details, input, select, dialog) before a custom widget.
rules.why: Native elements come with keyboard support, focus handling, form behaviour and screen-reader semantics. A custom widget has to rebuild all of that and usually misses some of it.
rules.check: No clickable div or span (onClick, role="button"); Tab reaches every control.
rules.anti_pattern: A div with onClick as a button, a script-driven accordion instead of details and summary, a custom toggle that isn't a radio or checkbox.

items.title: FAQ that answers real objections

rules.title: Links go, buttons do
rules.statement: Use a link to go to a URL and a button to act on the page; the style never decides.
rules.why: Links open in new tabs, can be copied and are announced as links; buttons submit and toggle. Using the wrong element breaks those expectations even when it looks right.
rules.check: Everything that navigates has an href and works with middle click; buttons only act.
rules.anti_pattern: A button that calls router.push() to navigate, or an anchor with href="#" that submits a form.
sources: docs/quality-gates.md (Interaction: links work with click, keyboard, modifier click and middle click)

rules.title: Compared options share rows
rules.statement: Give compared options the same rows in the same order, aligned, values written out.
rules.why: Comparison happens row by row. When each option lists different features in a different order, people have to rebuild the table in their heads.
rules.check: At 768 and up, each attribute lines up across options; values are text, not ticks.
rules.anti_pattern: Pricing cards with a dozen ticked features each, mostly repeated, in a different order per card and out of line.
sources: docs/v1.2/plan.md §6.2 (example: comparison rows over feature-tick soup)

items.title: Pricing tiers compared on the limits that matter

rules.title: No identical card grids
rules.statement: Shape each block by its content; don't force unlike content into identical icon cards.
rules.why: Identical icon cards make every point look equally important and equally vague. Evidence, comparisons, questions and steps each have a natural shape, and using it shows the content is real.
rules.check: Every grid of 3+ same-shaped cards holds true peers; otherwise use a list or table.
rules.anti_pattern: Three rounded cards with an icon, a two-word title and a line of filler each, for points that have nothing in common.
sources: docs/v1.2/plan.md §6.4 (feature default: three identical icon cards)
design.md §9 (avoid the repeated rounded card with shadow)
AGENTS.md §13, v1.1 (tag v1.1-archive): no oversized rounded wrappers as a substitute for hierarchy

rules.title: Headings make a specific point
rules.statement: Write headings that make the product's point, not labels like "Features" or "FAQ".
rules.why: A category label tells people what kind of section they are in, which they can already see. A specific heading tells them why to keep reading and still makes sense out of context.
rules.check: Swap in another product's name: if the heading still works, rewrite it.
rules.anti_pattern: "Features", "Why choose us?", "Frequently Asked Questions" and "Everything you need to succeed".
sources: AGENTS.md §13, v1.1 (tag v1.1-archive): no generic AI filler copy

rules.title: Action labels name the outcome
rules.statement: Label actions with what happens next, not "Get started", "Submit" or "Learn more".
rules.why: Specific labels let people predict the result before they commit, and they make sense to screen-reader users who list links and buttons out of context.
rules.check: Read each button and link out of context: it says what it does or where it goes.
rules.anti_pattern: "Get started" on every pricing card, "Submit" on every form, and rows of "Learn more" links.
sources: docs/v1.2/plan.md §6.2 (example default: the same CTA label on every card)

items.title: Empty state that says why and what next
Pricing tiers compared on the limits that matter

rules.title: No invented proof
rules.statement: Show no ratings, counts, logos, quotes or metrics you can't source.
rules.why: Invented proof is false the moment the component ships with it, and placeholder claims are routinely left in. Honest UI states only what is known.
rules.check: Trace every number, logo and quote to a real source, or label it fictional demo content.
rules.anti_pattern: "Trusted by 10,000+ teams", a row of placeholder logos, five-star ratings and testimonials from people who don't exist.
sources: docs/v1.2/plan.md §6.4 (social proof default: invented logos, metrics and testimonials)

rules.title: Answer first
rules.statement: Lead answers, errors and notices with the answer or consequence, then the detail.
rules.why: People scan. When the first words are the answer ("Yes.", "Nothing was deleted.") most readers can stop there; the detail is for those who need it.
rules.check: Read only the first sentence of each answer or message: it gives the answer or outcome.
rules.anti_pattern: FAQ answers that open with "Great question! At Acme we believe…" and errors that start with an apology and bury what happened.

items.title: FAQ that answers real objections

rules.title: Arrows only for leaving
rules.statement: Put an arrow on a link only when it leaves the site (↗), never on every link.
rules.why: An arrow on everything stops meaning anything. Kept for links that take people elsewhere, it warns them before they click.
rules.check: Every link or button with an arrow glyph or icon goes to another site or app.
rules.anti_pattern: "Learn more →" on every card, buttons with trailing arrows, and arrow icons on in-page actions.
sources: docs/v1.2/plan.md §4 (tells: arrows only where they mean "goes somewhere else")

rules.title: Every data region has its states
rules.statement: Design empty, loading and error states for every region that loads or lists data.
rules.why: Real data is often missing, slow or failing, especially on first use. A region designed only for the happy path shows a blank box or a broken layout exactly when people need guidance.
rules.check: Force no data, a slow network and a failed request: each shows a designed state.
rules.anti_pattern: A table or list that renders nothing, or spins forever, when the data is empty or the request fails.
sources: docs/quality-gates.md (Interaction: empty, error and loading states exist)
docs/v1.2/plan.md §6.4 (data table default: no empty, loading or error states)

items.title: Empty state that says why and what next

rules.title: Empty states differ by cause
rules.statement: Give first use, no results and failure their own message and action.
rules.why: Each cause needs a different next step: create something, change the search, or retry. One generic message makes people guess which situation they are in.
rules.check: First use, no matches and a failed load each show their own copy and action.
rules.anti_pattern: One illustration and "Nothing here yet" for an empty account, a mistyped search and a server error alike.
sources: docs/v1.2/plan.md §6.4 (empty-state default: illustration and "Nothing here yet")

items.title: Empty state that says why and what next

rules.title: State changes don't move the page
rules.statement: Reserve space so loading, toggles and validation don't shift surrounding content.
rules.why: Content that jumps makes people lose their place and click the wrong thing. Reserving room for text that appears keeps the page still.
rules.check: Switch every state at 1440 and 390: nothing else moves (CLS under 0.1).
rules.anti_pattern: Error text inserted above a field that pushes the form down, or a billing note that appears only for annual billing and shifts the buttons.

items.title: Pricing tiers compared on the limits that matter

rules.title: Errors explain and offer a way out
rules.statement: Say what failed, what is still safe, and one way forward (retry, edit or contact).
rules.why: An error without its consequences leaves people worried about their work; one without an action leaves them stuck. Both lead to repeated attempts and support requests.
rules.check: Trigger each error: the text names the failure, the impact and an action.
rules.anti_pattern: A red toast reading "Something went wrong" with no detail and no retry.

items.title: Empty state that says why and what next

rules.title: Destructive actions state consequences
rules.statement: Before a destructive action, name what is lost and if it can be undone; confirm it.
rules.why: Deletion is the one action people can't take back. Naming the object and the consequence turns an accidental click into a decision.
rules.check: Each delete or reset confirms with the object and consequence named; Cancel gets focus.
rules.anti_pattern: A red Delete button that acts at once, or an "Are you sure?" dialog with OK and Cancel and no word about what will be lost.
sources: docs/v1.2/plan.md §6.4 (settings default: delete with no confirmation or consequences)
WCAG 2.2 SC 3.3.4 Error Prevention (Legal, Financial, Data) (AA)
WAI-ARIA Authoring Practices Guide, Dialog (Modal) pattern

rules.title: Recompose for small screens
rules.statement: On phones, restack content by priority and adapt components; don't shrink the desktop.
rules.why: A scaled-down desktop keeps the desktop's order and density on a screen a third as wide. Recomposing puts the most important content and action first, at a usable size.
rules.check: At 390: priority order holds, nothing is cramped side by side, text is no smaller.
rules.anti_pattern: Three columns squeezed side by side on a phone, or a desktop table shrunk to tiny text.

rules.title: Reflow at 320 without sideways scroll
rules.statement: Fit every surface into 320 CSS px with no sideways scroll; only tables and code may scroll.
rules.why: 320 px is a 1280 px screen at 400% zoom, and the width of small phones. Scrolling sideways to read each line makes the page unusable for people who zoom.
rules.check: At 320 px, the document is no wider than the viewport and no text is clipped.
rules.anti_pattern: Fixed min-widths, long unbroken URLs or a row of nowrap buttons that pushes the page wider than the screen.

rules.title: Break where the content breaks
rules.statement: Change layout where the content stops fitting, not at device names.
rules.why: Screens come in every width. A layout that changes where its content needs room works at all of them; one tuned to "tablet" and "phone" breaks in between.
rules.check: Resize from 1440 to 320: no width crushes columns or orphans one card on a row.
rules.anti_pattern: Three pricing cards kept side by side down to 768px because that is the tablet breakpoint, squeezing each one to a narrow strip.
sources: design.md §12 (breakpoints are behaviour triggers, not device labels)

items.title: FAQ that answers real objections
Pricing tiers compared on the limits that matter

rules.title: Motion only explains change
rules.statement: Animate only changes people cause (open, close, switch); no decorative motion.
rules.why: Motion that follows an action shows what changed and where. Motion for its own sake competes with the content, delays reading and can make people feel unwell.
rules.check: Without interaction nothing moves, on load or scroll; transitions take 240ms or less.
rules.anti_pattern: Floating hero blobs, a fade-up on every section as it scrolls in, parallax backgrounds and cursor-follow effects.

items.title: FAQ that answers real objections

rules.title: Respect reduced motion
rules.statement: Under prefers-reduced-motion, remove non-essential transforms and transitions.
rules.why: For people with vestibular disorders, movement on screen can cause dizziness and nausea. The operating-system setting is how they ask for less.
rules.check: Emulate prefers-reduced-motion: reduce; only essential motion remains.
rules.anti_pattern: Slide-ins, parallax and animated counters that run whatever the reduced-motion setting says.

items.title: FAQ that answers real objections

rules.title: 44px touch targets
rules.statement: Make every interactive target at least 44×44 CSS px; inline text links excepted.
rules.why: Small targets cause mis-taps on touch screens and are hard to hit with a tremor or limited dexterity. WCAG's AA minimum is 24px; 44px is its enhanced level and the bar these rules use.
rules.check: At 390, every button, link and control's hit area is 44×44px or more, inline links aside.
rules.anti_pattern: 32px icon buttons, tiny close crosses and tightly packed pill filters.

items.title: Empty state that says why and what next

rules.title: Visible focus
rules.statement: Show a visible :focus-visible indicator on every interactive element.
rules.why: Keyboard users need to see where they are. Removing the outline without a replacement leaves them navigating blind.
rules.check: Tab through at 1440 and 390: each stop shows an uncovered indicator at 3:1 contrast.
rules.anti_pattern: outline: none in a global reset with no replacement, or a focus style that is only a faint colour change.

rules.title: AA contrast in every theme
rules.statement: Meet 4.5:1 for text and 3:1 for large text and control edges, in every theme.
rules.why: Muted grey on tinted surfaces is where contrast usually slips, and a pair that passes in the light theme can fail in the dark one. Checking every theme catches both.
rules.check: Run axe with the WCAG 2.2 AA tags in each theme: no contrast violations.
rules.anti_pattern: Light-grey helper text on an off-white card, or muted text that passes only on pure white.

rules.title: Label every control
rules.statement: Give every control a visible label, groups a legend, and errors a link to their field.
rules.why: Placeholders disappear as soon as people type and are not reliably announced. Visible labels, legends and linked errors tell everyone what a control is and what went wrong.
rules.check: Clicking a label focuses its control; groups have a legend; errors use aria-describedby.
rules.anti_pattern: Placeholder-only inputs, a row of radio buttons with no group label, and one error banner at the top of the form.
sources: docs/quality-gates.md (Accessibility: every field has a label; errors are connected to their controls)

rules.title: Announce changes in place
rules.statement: Announce results, saves and errors that appear in place through a polite live region.
rules.why: Sighted people see a result count change or a "Saved" message; screen-reader users hear nothing unless the change is announced.
rules.check: With a screen reader, filter, save and fail: each change is announced once, focus unmoved.
rules.anti_pattern: A result count that updates silently, or a toast that appears and disappears without being announced.
sources: docs/quality-gates.md (Accessibility: live regions announce search, filter and result changes)

rules.title: Keyboard complete, nothing hover-only
rules.statement: Make everything work by keyboard, close overlays on Escape, and hide nothing behind hover.
rules.why: Many people navigate by keyboard or switch device, and touch screens have no hover. Anything reachable only by mouse or hover is missing for them.
rules.check: Keyboard alone reaches and operates everything; Escape closes overlays and focus returns.
rules.anti_pattern: Menus that open only on hover, tooltips holding essential information, and dialogs that trap focus or drop it on close.
sources: WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.13 Content on Hover or Focus (AA)
docs/quality-gates.md (Interaction: menus close on Escape and return focus)

# Tessli UI rules

Tessli is an open-source UI library that ships its reasoning. These 39 rules cover structure and behaviour (hierarchy, spacing, states, copy, responsive, accessibility), not a visual style: keep your project's own theme.
Status: every rule is a draft until a maintainer signs it; 0 of 39 reviewed. Reasons and sources for each: https://tessli.vercel.app/rules
Use: read this before building UI. Then render at 1440, 768 and 390 px (and 320 px for overflow) and verify each rule's check.
Format: `ID rule | how to check`. Generated from rules/*.md; edit those, not this file.

## Hierarchy

- H-01 Give each section, card or dialog at most one primary-styled action. | Count primary-styled actions per section and dialog at 1440 and 390: one at most.
- H-02 One h1 per page; nest h2–h4 in order. Level follows structure, size follows style. | Run axe heading-order or list the outline: one h1, no skipped levels.
- H-03 Use at most one uppercase eyebrow per page, and only if it adds information. | Count uppercase, letter-spaced labels over headings: one per page at most.
- H-04 Use numbered markers (01, 02, Step 1) only for steps people follow in order. | For each numbered marker: does order matter to the user? If not, drop the numbers.

## Typography

- T-01 Cap running text at a readable measure (about 65ch), never the full container width. | At 1440, every body paragraph has a max-width of 80ch or less.
- T-02 Take font sizes from the type scale; use at most four sizes in one section. | List computed font sizes per section at 1440 and 390: all on the scale, four at most.
- T-03 Set prices, counts and numeric columns in tabular figures. | Inspect prices, counts and numeric columns: font-variant-numeric is tabular-nums.

## Spacing and density

- S-01 Keep space inside a group smaller than space between groups, at every width. | Measure gaps at 1440 and 390: label to content < item to item < section to section.
- S-02 Align a section's heading, text and actions on one left edge; centre only short blocks. | At 1440, heading, text and actions share a left edge; centred text runs 3 lines at most.
- S-03 Make data surfaces compact and reading surfaces roomy; don't use one density everywhere. | At 1440×900, data rows are 48px tall or less; reading text has line-height 1.5 or more.

## Colour

- C-01 Colour with semantic tokens (background, primary, muted, border…), never raw values. | No hex, rgb(), hsl() or palette classes in the component; it works in light and dark.
- C-02 Pair every colour-coded meaning (error, selected, status) with text or shape. | View it in greyscale: every state is still identifiable from text or shape.
- C-03 Spend the primary colour on the primary action and real status, not decoration. | At 1440 and 390, every element in the primary colour is the primary action or a status.
- C-04 Show importance with position, size, weight and borders, not gradients, glows or glass. | Search the styles for gradients, blur and backdrop-filter: none carries meaning.

## Components

- K-01 Use the native element (button, a, details, input, select, dialog) before a custom widget. | No clickable div or span (onClick, role="button"); Tab reaches every control.
- K-02 Use a link to go to a URL and a button to act on the page; the style never decides. | Everything that navigates has an href and works with middle click; buttons only act.
- K-03 Give compared options the same rows in the same order, aligned, values written out. | At 768 and up, each attribute lines up across options; values are text, not ticks.
- K-04 Shape each block by its content; don't force unlike content into identical icon cards. | Every grid of 3+ same-shaped cards holds true peers; otherwise use a list or table.

## Copy

- W-01 Write headings that make the product's point, not labels like "Features" or "FAQ". | Swap in another product's name: if the heading still works, rewrite it.
- W-02 Label actions with what happens next, not "Get started", "Submit" or "Learn more". | Read each button and link out of context: it says what it does or where it goes.
- W-03 Show no ratings, counts, logos, quotes or metrics you can't source. | Trace every number, logo and quote to a real source, or label it fictional demo content.
- W-04 Lead answers, errors and notices with the answer or consequence, then the detail. | Read only the first sentence of each answer or message: it gives the answer or outcome.
- W-05 Put an arrow on a link only when it leaves the site (↗), never on every link. | Every link or button with an arrow glyph or icon goes to another site or app.

## States

- ST-01 Design empty, loading and error states for every region that loads or lists data. | Force no data, a slow network and a failed request: each shows a designed state.
- ST-02 Give first use, no results and failure their own message and action. | First use, no matches and a failed load each show their own copy and action.
- ST-03 Reserve space so loading, toggles and validation don't shift surrounding content. | Switch every state at 1440 and 390: nothing else moves (CLS under 0.1).
- ST-04 Say what failed, what is still safe, and one way forward (retry, edit or contact). | Trigger each error: the text names the failure, the impact and an action.
- ST-05 Before a destructive action, name what is lost and if it can be undone; confirm it. | Each delete or reset confirms with the object and consequence named; Cancel gets focus.

## Responsive

- R-01 On phones, restack content by priority and adapt components; don't shrink the desktop. | At 390: priority order holds, nothing is cramped side by side, text is no smaller.
- R-02 Fit every surface into 320 CSS px with no sideways scroll; only tables and code may scroll. | At 320 px, the document is no wider than the viewport and no text is clipped.
- R-03 Change layout where the content stops fitting, not at device names. | Resize from 1440 to 320: no width crushes columns or orphans one card on a row.

## Motion

- M-01 Animate only changes people cause (open, close, switch); no decorative motion. | Without interaction nothing moves, on load or scroll; transitions take 240ms or less.
- M-02 Under prefers-reduced-motion, remove non-essential transforms and transitions. | Emulate prefers-reduced-motion: reduce; only essential motion remains.

## Accessibility

- A-01 Make every interactive target at least 44×44 CSS px; inline text links excepted. | At 390, every button, link and control's hit area is 44×44px or more, inline links aside.
- A-02 Show a visible :focus-visible indicator on every interactive element. | Tab through at 1440 and 390: each stop shows an uncovered indicator at 3:1 contrast.
- A-03 Meet 4.5:1 for text and 3:1 for large text and control edges, in every theme. | Run axe with the WCAG 2.2 AA tags in each theme: no contrast violations.
- A-04 Give every control a visible label, groups a legend, and errors a link to their field. | Clicking a label focuses its control; groups have a legend; errors use aria-describedby.
- A-05 Announce results, saves and errors that appear in place through a polite live region. | With a screen reader, filter, save and fail: each change is announced once, focus unmoved.
- A-06 Make everything work by keyboard, close overlays on Escape, and hide nothing behind hover. | Keyboard alone reaches and operates everything; Escape closes overlays and focus returns.
